blocks.text: **Context.** Ownly is Rapido's food-delivery app. It is reported to charge restaurants no commission and customers no platform fee, and it is prepaid only {{SECONDARY}}. It runs three apps: customer, restaurant partner, and captain (rider).

**Problem discovered.** Across 1,000 customer reviews (27 Sep–4 Oct 2026), the worst-rated experience is not slow food or a bad menu. It is **paying and getting nothing**: the order is cancelled after payment, no captain arrives, or the order is marked “Delivered” without a handover. 156 of 493 negative reviews (31.6%) describe one of these. When they do, the rating is ~1★ whether or not support is also mentioned {{ACTUAL}}.

**Why it matters.** Ownly's advantage is price, and that is working: even 42 angry reviewers still praise it. But a prepaid, low-margin model cannot absorb a failed order. Every failure costs the full order value plus support time, and generates public “fraud” language (74 negative reviews use fraud/scam wording) {{ACTUAL}}. Since July 2026 Rapido's app sends new users to Ownly {{SECONDARY}}, so a failure is also a failure of Rapido's distribution.

**Triangulation.** The restaurant and captain apps describe the same breakdowns from the other side: order alerts that don't ring so orders auto-cancel, captains sent too early, and opaque captain incentive rules. All three apps share one pattern: a manual queue with no visible status and no owner {{INFERENCE}}.
**Root-cause hypothesis.** No step in the order pipeline has to *prove* a handoff happened, and no rule makes the customer whole automatically when one fails {{HYPOTHESIS}}.

**Business impact.** Cannot be sized from public data. The severe-failure rate per order and the repeat-order gap after a failure are both {{UNKNOWN}}. The sensitivity model (Section 12) shows the direct financial return is small at Ownly's thin margin, so the case rests on retention, trust and Rapido brand protection. That makes **sizing the failure rate the first deliverable**, before building anything.

**Recommendation and MVP.** Run a 2-week sizing gate. If severe failures are at least 1% of orders, or the 30-day repeat gap is 10 percentage points or more, build **Ownly Promise v1**: a 4-digit delivery code the captain must enter to mark an order delivered, plus three automatic refund rules (cancelled after payment, no captain within 20 minutes, “not received” on an unverified delivery). Every failure is logged with a cause code.

**Validation and success metric.** A zone-randomised pilot in one city (Bengaluru, subject to data) for at least 4 weeks. **Primary KPI:** “not received” claims per 1,000 delivered orders. **North Star:** weekly *promise-kept orders*. **Guardrails:** captain food-order acceptance, handover time, refund cost and abuse rate. Scale on a ≥40% drop with healthy guardrails; reject at <15%.

blocks.text: Marketplace structure

Ownly coordinates three sides it does not fully control. A customer pays upfront; the restaurant must accept and prepare the order; a captain must collect and hand it over. Ownly's operations sit in the middle and handle support, refunds, onboarding and dispatch.
Exhibit 1. Ownly's three-sided marketplace and the three handoffs named in reviews.
Economics that matter for this problem

Incumbents (Swiggy, Zomato) are reported to earn 15–30% commission plus a ₹15–18 platform fee {{SECONDARY}}. Ownly gives most of that up and earns mainly the delivery fee. **Inference:** Ownly's margin per order is thin and roughly fixed, so a failed order (refund + support + captain time) can wipe out the margin of many good orders. A commission model has more room to absorb failures. This is why reliability is more important to Ownly's model than to the incumbents' {{INFERENCE}}.

blocks.title: The economics are not verified
lines: Contribution per order, delivery cost per trip and refund cost are not public. This document uses ₹5 / ₹10 / ₹15 contribution scenarios and a ~₹30 fee only to show how sensitive the conclusion is. Replace them with finance data before any build decision.

blocks.text: Competitive context in one line

Ownly wins on price and, on the evidence, loses on reliability and support. Customers say so directly: *“Zomato, Swiggy is way more good than this”* (1★, 2 Oct 2026). One reviewer praises the pricing *“in the age of institutionalised fleecing by Swiggy and Zomato”* and in the same review calls customer service useless (1★, 4 Oct 2026) {{OBSERVATION}}.
Why this problem could matter strategically

items: **Price is the moat, reliability is the leak.** Incumbents can improve reliability more easily than they can drop commission, which would cut into their own profit. Ownly needs to be reliable enough, not best in class {{INFERENCE}}.

**Rapido's distribution makes first orders the moment of truth.** Rapido users arrive at Ownly through its super-app. If their first order fails, that distribution is wasted. First-order reviews average 2.05★ (n=22) {{ACTUAL}}, a small sample.
**Brand spillover.** 14 customer reviews name Rapido, 10 of them negative, e.g. *“side gig in between rapido rides”* {{ACTUAL}}. A food failure is also a Rapido brand risk.

blocks.text: Why multiple sources were necessary

items: **Reviews alone over-sample anger.** A customer whose order worked rarely writes 40 words; a customer who lost ₹430 does. The restaurant and captain apps test whether the customer story has a real operational mechanism behind it.

**Different sides see different halves of one failure.** A customer sees “cancelled after payment”. A restaurant sees “the ring didn't fire, the order auto-cancelled, and I was blamed”. Only together do they point to a cause.
**Search data tests the growth alternative.** If discovery were the constraint, it would show up as a search gap. It does, but the data shows distribution runs through Rapido, not search (Section 8).

blocks.text: Method in four steps

items: **Code** every review into themes (keyword dictionary for customer and captain apps; analyst coding for the restaurant app) and map themes to journey stages.
**Measure** each theme on frequency (share of 1–2★ reviews), severity (average rating when mentioned), agreement (thumbs-up), recency and segment.
**Stress-test** the coding: check false positives, re-cut the strongest claims, and drop any claim that does not survive (Appendix C).
**Triangulate**: promote a pattern only if an independent source shows the same mechanism, then write competing hypotheses before choosing one.

blocks.text: The failure cascade
Exhibit 6. Within negative reviews: operational failure → no recovery → brand-damage language.

61% of negative reviews describe an operational failure; two-thirds of those also say they could not get help or a refund; and 43 go on to use fraud/scam words or name a competitor {{ACTUAL}}. The cascade shows the order of events in the review text. It does **not** prove that the lack of recovery caused the brand damage (see the correction below).
Exhibit 7. Average rating by failure type, split by whether support/refund is also criticised.

blocks.title: Recovery does not rescue a severe failure
lines: An earlier analysis concluded that “failed recovery costs a full star” (2.33★ vs 1.07★). Split by failure type, that gap disappears for severe failures: cancelled orders are 1.00★ either way, and not-delivered orders are 1.08★ vs 1.05★. The gap only exists for delays and food quality. Even there, the “no recovery complaint” group is inflated by false positives: 53 of those 159 reviews are 4–5★, and the delay dictionary includes positive phrases such as “on time” and “punctual”.
**Implication:** prevent the severe failure first. Recovery is necessary but will not save the rating on its own.

lines: H1 has the strongest triangulated evidence and the clearest mechanism. But a strong signal in reviews is not proof of business impact. What the model says, honestly

items: **Direct contribution is small.** Even in the upside case, extra contribution from retention is ~₹1.6L per monthly cohort per 10k orders/day. On direct financial return alone, the MVP would be hard to justify {{ESTIMATE}}.

**Who bears F depends on today's refund policy.** If the customer currently absorbs a false delivery (no refund), F is a customer loss that becomes churn, not an Ownly saving. If Ownly refunds it, F is a direct saving. The split is {{UNKNOWN}}.

**The real return is unmodelled:** store conversion (detailed 1★ reviews are what prospective users read), Rapido brand protection, and restaurant volume (GMV retained flows to restaurants that are deciding whether to keep the Ownly tablet on).
**The two numbers that decide everything are f and the repeat gap.** Below f = 0.5% with a repeat gap under 5 pp, this is a CX fix, not a strategy.

blocks.text: What competitors do better

items: Resolve problems and support restaurants. Both customers and partners say so in their own words {{OBSERVATION}}.
Run delivery with dedicated fleets and handling standards {{REQUIRES VALIDATION}}.
Brand trust and search presence: ~1,000× Ownly's modelled organic traffic {{ACTUAL}}.

blocks.text: What competitors do worse

items: Price. Customers explicitly contrast Ownly's pricing with incumbents' fees {{OBSERVATION}}.
Restaurant take rate. Commission is their profit pool, so matching Ownly's zero-commission offer would hurt them {{INFERENCE}}.

blocks.text: Opportunity and realistic differentiation
Ownly cannot out-spend incumbents on brand, and does not need to beat them on speed. Two things it can realistically own:

items: **Fair price** (already working), which incumbents cannot easily copy without cutting into their profit.

**A verifiable handover** built on a habit Rapido's users and captains may already have. Rapido rides start with a code the rider shares {{REQUIRES VALIDATION}}: widely understood, but not verified in this research. If true, a delivery code is a native behaviour on Ownly's network rather than new friction.

blocks.title: Positioning
lines: “The fair-price food app you can trust with your money.” Fair price is working. Trust is the missing half, and it is cheaper for Ownly to build trust than for incumbents to copy fair pricing {{INFERENCE}}.

blocks.text: RICE was used as a first pass. Reach is an index (100 = all orders in a quarter); Impact 0.25–3; Confidence 0–1; Effort in person-months. All inputs are {{ESTIMATE}}s and are relative, not precise.
RICE = Reach × Impact × Confidence ÷ Effort. Example: S1 = 100 × 2 × 0.7 ÷ 3 = 46.7.
Exhibit 13. Value against the root cause vs complexity. Positions are judgement, consistent with the RICE inputs.
Why the framework does not make the decision

items: **RICE ranks cheap cosmetic fixes first** (S8 = 80) because they reach everyone. They should ship, but they do not touch the root cause.

**RICE ranks auto-refund low** (10.5) because few orders fail. Yet it addresses the single moment that creates fraud language, and it is what makes a delivery code visible as protection to the customer.

**S1 and S2 are a system, not two features.** The code makes generous auto-refunds affordable, because “not received” claims become checkable. The auto-refund makes the code meaningful to the customer. Shipping one without the other weakens both.
**S3 tests a different cause** (restaurant alerts) and needs no captain-app change, so it runs as a separate, cheaper experiment rather than inflating the MVP.

blocks.title: Selected: S1 + S2 (incl. S4's timeout as rule R2) as the MVP
lines: It is the smallest intervention that tests the core hypothesis: verifying the handoff and resolving failures automatically reduces paid-no-food losses and protects repeat ordering. blocks.text: User stories and acceptance criteria

head: **User story**
**Acceptance criteria (Given / When / Then)**
rows: As a customer, when my food arrives I share a code, so nobody can claim it was delivered when it wasn't

Given an order is picked up, when I open tracking, then I see a 4-digit code and the copy “Share only when food is in your hands”. When the captain enters the correct code, the status becomes “Delivered – verified” within 2 s
As a customer whose order was cancelled after I paid, I see my money back without asking
Given a non-customer cancellation, when it is recorded, then a refund is issued within 60 s and the receipt shows amount, destination, time and reason
As a customer with no captain after 20 min, I choose whether to wait or cancel
Given acceptance + 20 min with no captain, then I get a push and an in-app card with “Cancel · refund ₹X” and “Keep waiting (new ETA)”
As a captain, I can finish a delivery when the customer doesn't answer
Given 2 unanswered calls and 3 min at the drop point, when I take a photo within 75 m of the pin, then the order closes as “Delivered – unverified”
As an ops analyst, I can see every failure with its cause
Every cancellation, refund and unverified delivery has a cause code and owner; a daily export reconciles to order counts within 0.5%

blocks.text: Edge cases

items: Order placed for someone else → share the code to the recipient's number via SMS or WhatsApp.
Gated community or guard handover → the guard reads out the code; otherwise fallback.
Customer's phone is dead → fallback (photo + GPS).
Captain reassigned mid-trip → the code stays valid; the event is logged.
Captain asks for the code before arriving (“I'm downstairs”) → GPS distance is checked when the code is entered; copy warns the customer.
Partial or wrong items → out of scope; existing flow.
Repeat “not received” claimants → R3 cap; device and account linking.

blocks.text: Dependencies and risks

items: **Captain app release** (critical path). Whether Ownly controls the Ownly Captain app end-to-end, or needs Rapido's captain app, is {{REQUIRES VALIDATION}}.
**Payments** for instant wallet credit; **Legal** for refund terms; **CX** for the policy change.
**Top risk:** captains quietly decline food orders because the code removes shortcuts. This would turn false deliveries into no-captain failures. It is treated as a hard guardrail (Section 20).

blocks.text: Exhibit 15. Key screens: entry point (A), core interaction (B), failure state (C), recovery/success state (D).

head: **Screen**
**Purpose**
**UX decision and reasoning**
rows: A · Order on the way (entry point)
Introduce the code at the moment it matters

Code shown large on the tracking screen, **not only in SMS**, so it is available offline and visible to the person waiting. Copy explains *why* before asking: “Share only when food is in your hands”. That turns the code into protection rather than friction.
B · Captain at the door (core interaction)
Make verification as quick as starting a ride

Mirrors a familiar 4-box code entry pattern (assumed similar to ride start; {{REQUIRES VALIDATION}}). The fallback is visible but secondary, unlocked only after 2 calls, so it is not the default path.
Give control back at the worst moment
Shown proactively at 20 min, before the customer has to search for help. Two clear choices; the refund amount is stated, not “initiated”. A new ETA is shown if they choose to wait.

A refund is shown as a completed fact with amount, destination, time, reference and reason, which directly answers the “refund stuck in initiated” complaint. Ends with “Order again” to support the repeat behaviour.

blocks.title: Design principle
lines: Every screen answers one of three questions the reviews show customers cannot answer today: *Is my food really with me? Where is my money? What happens next?* Visual design is deliberately plain; the work is in the states and the copy.

blocks.title: Gate A comes first: E0 sizing (weeks 1–2, not an A/B test)
lines: Pull (1) the severe-failure rate per 1,000 orders by type and (2) the 30-day repeat rate of customers whose first order failed vs those whose first order was clean.

**Proceed at full scope** if severe failures are ≥ 1% of orders **or** the repeat gap is ≥ 10 pp. **Stop and pivot** to the retention/selection hypothesis (H9) if failures are < 0.5% **and** the gap is < 5 pp. In between: ship R1 + ledger + quick wins only, and re-read in 30 days.

**E1 · Ownly Promise v1**
rows: If the handover requires the customer's code and eligible failures auto-refund, then “not received” claims per 1,000 delivered orders fall by ≥ 40%, and failed-order customers' 30-day repeat moves closer to clean-order customers', because false deliveries become impossible to hide and money-loss moments resolve in minutes
Cluster-randomised controlled trial by delivery zone (not by user: captains and restaurants are shared within a zone, so user-level randomisation would leak)
Code at handover + R1–R3 + receipt screen
All prepaid orders in ≥ 6 matched zone pairs in the pilot city (Bengaluru, subject to E0 volume)

Illustrative: baseline claim rate 1.5%, target 50% relative cut (to 0.75%), α = 0.05, power 0.8 → n ≈ 7.84 × [0.015×0.985 + 0.0075×0.9925] ÷ 0.0075² ≈ **3,100 orders per arm** before clustering. With a design effect of 2–3 → **~6,200–9,300 per arm**. Recompute with the real baseline from E0
≥ 4 weeks (two full weekly cycles plus captain adaptation); repeat-rate read at day 30–45 after the pilot start
Delivered-without-GPS-match %; refund latency; refund cost per 1,000 orders; 30-day repeat of failed-order customers; fraud/scam language per 1,000 orders in post-order feedback

Captain food-order acceptance (≤ 5% relative drop); median handover time added (≤ 45 s); fallback usage (≤ 15% of deliveries); refund abuse rate (≤ 2% of auto-refunds); delivery time; contribution per order after refunds (≤ ₹3 drop)
≥ 40% relative drop in primary metric with all guardrails intact
Rain or festivals; city-wide promos; Rapido incentive changes; novelty effects. Mitigated by matched pairs and difference-in-differences against the pre-period

blocks.text: Second-order effects

items: **Positive loop (expected):** verified handovers → fewer paid-no-food orders → fewer fraud reviews → more repeat orders → more orders per restaurant → partners keep the tablet on and accept faster → fewer cancellations {{HYPOTHESIS}}.
**The loop may currently run in reverse:** partners report “one order a day”, may deprioritise the tablet, miss alerts, and cause cancellations that suppress demand {{INFERENCE}}.
**Liability attribution changes behaviour on all sides.** Once failures are charged to the party at fault, marginal partners may leave. That improves quality but reduces listed selection.

**Inversion: how to guarantee failure.** Market the Promise before the code works; pay captains per code so costs explode; set loose refund rules that spread on WhatsApp; ignore restaurant-side cancellations so the refund bill grows. The plan is built to avoid each.

head: **Area**
**Learning**
rows: Customers come for price and forgive slowness; they do not forgive losing money. The emotional break point is “I paid and nobody helped”, which they express as “fraud”.
The weakest part of the product is not a screen; it is the absence of proof at handoffs and of automatic recovery. Every side, including captains and restaurants, is stuck in an invisible queue.
Zero commission makes reliability existential: there is little margin to absorb failures. Direct ROI from fixing them is modest; the value is retention, trust and Rapido's brand.

“Failed recovery costs a full star” (does not hold for severe failures); “94% of helpful votes sit on complaints” (true, but n = 32); “not enough captains” (contradicted by idle and paused-onboarding signals; reframed); “SEO is a growth lever” (distribution runs through Rapido).
Failure rate per order; repeat gap; causes of cancellations; who controls the captain app; competitor recovery flows; iOS and non-reviewer sentiment.
Request two queries (severe-failure rate and repeat gap) and decide at Gate A on day 14. Build nothing irreversible before then.

blocks.title: Final quality check
lines: **Is the problem proven?** Its existence and severity are, through multiple sources. Its size is not, which is why the plan starts with sizing.
**Could something else explain the evidence?** Yes: abuse, H9 (weak retention regardless), restaurant-side causes. Each has a test.
**Is the MVP small and testable?** Two mechanisms plus instrumentation, one city, pre-registered thresholds.
**Any invented facts?** No internal metrics are claimed; every number is labelled; four earlier claims were corrected (Appendix C).
